newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe sees investor boost from World Bank news.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe sees investor boost from World Bank news.

text.p: Barring drought, Zimbabwe's share market should end the year at record highs, encouraged by the World Bank's resumption this week of key aid to Harare after a two-year suspension, bourse officials said on Friday.

They said the World Bank announcement late on Thursday that it was releasing $62.5 million in balance-of-payments aid to Zimbabwe would boost investor confidence in the southern African country, especially among foreigners who had been spooked by suspension of aid by the Bank and other Western donors and, more recently, the multi-lateral lenders' withdrawal from Kenya.

Zimbabwe Stock Exchange (ZSE) chairman Mark Tunmer, chief executive Anthony Barfoot and some economic analysts said they expected other Western donors who also withheld aid from Harare in 1995 after it failed to meet some key cost-saving targets, to follow the World Bank's cue.
"Obviously it (resumption of World Bank aid) is very positive," Tunmer told Reuters.

"Perhaps there won't be an immediate impact on the market but it will give a lot more confidence and optimism to the foreign investors who were very nervous because they have seen what's happened in the past few weeks in Kenya," he said.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a key loan programme to Kenya on July 31 after a row over corruption.

"Two weeks after the IMF...pulled out of Kenya, they resume aid to Zimbabwe, it gives us a stamp of approval which is very important and will influence investors who are here to stay and those who were sitting on the fence will be a lot more optimistic," Tunmer said.

Barfoot said in a separate interview he expected the good news about the resumption of World Bank aid to offset "bad news" about an early buildup of the El Nino weather phenomenon which might spell drought for southern Africa this year.
"If we get some reasonable early rains in November and December we should still see the market closing the year around the 13,000 (point) level," Tunmer said.
The exchange's main industrial index, which has scaled record highs in the past month, ended Thursday at 12,001.03.

World Bank deputy resident representative Kapil Kapoor told reporters the Bank reached the decision to resume aid last week after reviewing Zimbabwe's macroeconomic performance and its 18-month 1997/98 budget presented on July 24.

The bank's chief representative to Harare David Cook told Reuters last month that on the face of it Zimbabwe's latest budget -- which had a surprise reduction in the government deficit -- looked favourable both for the release of the $62.5 million and for general support for a second leg of economic reforms due to be launched later this year.
Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa announced an unexpected fall in the government's spending deficit for the 1996/97 financial year ended June 30 to 7.1 percent of Gross Domestic Product.
This not only met but was also below -- for the first time in seven years -- the government-set target of 8.5 percent.

However, Tunmer and some analysts said the government should now act on pledges it made in the budget to whittle the deficit further and keep a lid on annual inflation -- running at 19.1 percent in July compared with 21.4 percent in June.
Short-term interest rates on the local money market eased on Friday with dealers forecasting they would slip further on the back of the World Bank's announcement and the lower inflation figure.
Stock market brokers said the lower money market rates should lead to more interest in equities.
